text: It was not, she presently came to feel, that he had said anything which a person of her own deliberate scruple could have fixed upon as wanting; it was rather, and far more disturbingly, that the very smoothness of his accommodation, the way in which he had, as it were, anticipated her hesitations and gathered them up into the larger ease of his manner, left her with the sense of having been spared a difficulty she would, on the whole, have been glad to encounter. She should have liked, she told herself, walking the long shaded room while the afternoon thinned about the window-seats, to have been resisted a little, to have had the chance of measuring against some honest opposition the strength of what she still, in her private and unconfessed way, supposed herself to want; and the absence of that friction, so far from reassuring her, became the one thing in the whole arrangement that she found she could not, by any amount of grateful reflection, manage altogether to forgive. There were moments, indeed, when his perfect considerateness struck her as the subtlest form a withholding could assume.

What he had come, in the end, to recognise in the old man's silence was not, he should have been the first to insist, anything so coarse as displeasure, nor yet that milder thing, a mere fatigue of attention; it was, if one were to be exact—and he found himself, in those slow evenings of the failing season, painfully committed to exactness—a kind of large and patient withdrawal, the gesture of a person who has decided, on grounds too delicate to be stated, that the conversation may now proceed perfectly well without him. He had wished, naturally, to be of use; he had offered, in a manner he supposed unmistakable, the whole of his disinterested attendance; and it was precisely the courteous completeness with which the offer had been received, and not refused, and somehow set aside, that made him understand, by degrees, how very far outside the real transaction he had all the while been standing. The knowledge came to him without bitterness, as such knowledge, at his age, was apt to come—rather, he reflected, as a faint coolness comes in at an opened door, perceptible only to those who had been warm.

She had supposed, in coming abroad, that the distance would do for her what her own resolution had so conspicuously failed to do; that the mere interposition of seas and unfamiliar tongues would dissolve, or at the least attenuate, the particular obligation under which she had, with an imprudence she now could only marvel at, allowed herself to be placed. It was therefore with something like consternation, mitigated by the irony she had learned to keep always at hand against herself, that she discovered the thing to have travelled with her—to be present, indeed, more vividly in the bright impersonal hotels and the gilded indifferent galleries than it had ever contrived to be at home, where a hundred small duties had at least the merit of crowding it for hours together out of sight. Here there was nothing to crowd it; here, in the leisure she had so expensively purchased, it sat with her at the small table, accompanied her along the river, and rose, faithful and unhurried, to meet her each morning at the window—so that she came to wonder whether what one fled were ever, in the nature of the case, the thing one had any real hope of leaving behind.

The house itself, he would afterwards maintain, had been the first to tell him; not in any vulgar way of creaking boards or significant portraits, but through that finer medium, the disposition of its rooms, which seemed to have been contrived—by what hand, and toward what end, he was at no early stage prepared to say—for the express purpose of keeping certain of its occupants forever just beyond the range of certain others. One passed, in that civil and beautifully kept interior, from the drawing-room to the conservatory, from the conservatory to the long gallery, with the smooth sense of being conducted; and it was only later, piecing together the small evidences as a man pieces a torn letter, that he perceived how each of these graceful transitions had also been, for the two persons whose nearness he had so wished to bring about, an occasion quietly and infallibly missed. The architecture, in short, conspired; and he, who had fancied himself the manager of the affair, came at last to suspect that he had been, from the threshold onward, no more than the most assiduous of its dupes.

I should be glad, even now, to be able to record that she met the disclosure with the composure her whole previous bearing had taught us to expect; but the truth, which I owe rather to my respect for her than to any appetite for the dramatic, is that she met it with no bearing at all, that the practised surface simply, for the space of a breath, was not there, and that what looked through the gap—before the admirable discipline of years could reassemble itself—was a thing so young, so nakedly and unguardedly hopeful, that I have been ashamed ever since to have been the person privileged to see it. She recovered, of course; she said the right, the almost too perfectly right, thing; she even, a moment after, found within herself the resource of a small laugh against her own surprise. Yet I carried away from that hour the conviction, which nothing in our subsequent and carefully smoothed intercourse has ever availed to shake, that I had surprised the one truth she had spent her considerable art in arranging that no one should ever be allowed to surprise.
